Base directory for this skill: /Users/vorcigernix/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/5.1.0/skills/subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Two-stage review after each task: spec compliance first, then code quality
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [shape=box];
        "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer subagent asks questions?";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?";
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?";
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [label="yes"];
    "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Prompt Templates

- `./implementer-prompt.md` - Dispatch implementer subagent
- `./spec-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch spec compliance reviewer subagent
- `./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Extract all 5 tasks with full text and context]
[Create TodoWrite with all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Get Task 1 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: "Got it. Implementing now..."
[Later] Implementer:
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant - all requirements met, nothing extra

[Get git SHAs, dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Approved.

[Mark Task 1 complete]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Get Task 2 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: [No questions, proceeds]
Implementer:
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Self-review: All good
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ❌ Issues:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  - Extra: Added --json flag (not requested)

[Implementer fixes issues]
Implementer: Removed --json flag, added progress reporting

[Spec reviewer reviews again]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant now

[Dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Solid. Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Implementer fixes]
Implementer: Extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant

[Code reviewer reviews again]
Code reviewer: ✅ Approved

[Mark Task 2 complete]

...

[After all tasks]
[Dispatch final code-reviewer]
Final reviewer: All requirements met, ready to merge

Done!
```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

## Integration

**Required workflow skills:**
- **superpowers:using-git-worktrees** - Ensures isolated workspace (creates one or verifies existing)
- **superpowers:writing-plans** - Creates the plan this skill executes
- **superpowers:requesting-code-review** - Code review template for reviewer subagents
- **superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch** - Complete development after all tasks

**Subagents should use:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - Subagents follow TDD for each task

**Alternative workflow:**
- **superpowers:executing-plans** - Use for parallel session instead of same-session execution

Now executing the plan via fresh subagents with per-task spec + quality review. We're already on the `sidebar-navigationsplitview` feature branch (not main), so isolation is fine — I'll execute in this checkout rather than a separate worktree, since the CEF/synced-Xcode build is path-sensitive.

The rail code it includes gets removed in Task 4 — honest, readable history. Recommended for subagent-driven review.

# Implementer Subagent Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching an implementer subagent.

```
Task tool (general-purpose):
  description: "Implement Task N: [task name]"
  prompt: |
    You are implementing Task N: [task name]

    ## Task Description

    [FULL TEXT of task from plan - paste it here, don't make subagent read file]

    ## Context

    [Scene-setting: where this fits, dependencies, architectural context]

    ## Before You Begin

    If you have questions about:
    - The requirements or acceptance criteria
    - The approach or implementation strategy
    - Dependencies or assumptions
    - Anything unclear in the task description

    **Ask them now.** Raise any concerns before starting work.

    ## Your Job

    Once you're clear on requirements:
    1. Implement exactly what the task specifies
    2. Write tests (following TDD if task says to)
    3. Verify implementation works
    4. Commit your work
    5. Self-review (see below)
    6. Report back

    Work from: [directory]

    **While you work:** If you encounter something unexpected or unclear, **ask questions**.
    It's always OK to pause and clarify. Don't guess or make assumptions.

    ## Code Organization

    You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more
    reliable when files are focused. Keep this in mind:
    - Follow the file structure defined in the plan
    - Each file should have one clear responsibility with a well-defined interface
    - If a file you're creating is growing beyond the plan's intent, stop and report
      it as DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — don't split files on your own without plan guidance
    - If an existing file you're modifying is already large or tangled, work carefully
      and note it as a concern in your report
    - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. Improve code you're touching
      the way a good developer would, but don't restructure things outside your task.

    ## When You're in Over Your Head

    It is always OK to stop and say "this is too hard for me." Bad work is worse than
    no work. You will not be penalized for escalating.

    **STOP and escalate when:**
    - The task requires architectural decisions with multiple valid approaches
    - You need to understand code beyond what was provided and can't find clarity
    - You feel uncertain about whether your approach is correct
    - The task involves restructuring existing code in ways the plan didn't anticipate
    - You've been reading file after file trying to understand the system without progress

    **How to escalate:** Report back with status BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT. Describe
    specifically what you're stuck on, what you've tried, and what kind of help you need.
    The controller can provide more context, re-dispatch with a more capable model,
    or break the task into smaller pieces.

    ## Before Reporting Back: Self-Review

    Review your work with fresh eyes. Ask yourself:

    **Completeness:**
    - Did I fully implement everything in the spec?
    - Did I miss any requirements?
    - Are there edge cases I didn't handle?

    **Quality:**
    - Is this my best work?
    - Are names clear and accurate (match what things do, not how they work)?
    - Is the code clean and maintainable?

    **Discipline:**
    - Did I avoid overbuilding (YAGNI)?
    - Did I only build what was requested?
    - Did I follow existing patterns in the codebase?

    **Testing:**
    - Do tests actually verify behavior (not just mock behavior)?
    - Did I follow TDD if required?
    - Are tests comprehensive?

    If you find issues during self-review, fix them now before reporting.

    ## Report Format

    When done, report:
    - **Status:** DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
    - What you implemented (or what you attempted, if blocked)
    - What you tested and test results
    - Files changed
    - Self-review findings (if any)
    - Any issues or concerns

    Use DONE_WITH_CONCERNS if you completed the work but have doubts about correctness.
    Use BLOCKED if you cannot complete the task. Use NEEDS_CONTEXT if you need
    information that wasn't provided. Never silently produce work you're unsure about.
```

- **Clarity:** Names accurate, doc comments meaningful, no dead code.
- **Discipline:** No overbuild, no SwiftUI import, no stray files, follows the surrounding code style.

Report in this format:
- **Strengths:** …

content.text:
Exactly two files, no other modifications.

---

**Strengths:**

- The `moving` helper faithfully re-implements SwiftUI's `RangeReplaceableCollection.move(fromOffsets:toOffset:)` semantics: items are collected before removal, removed in descending-index order (preventing index shift errors), and `insertionIndex` is correctly adjusted by subtracting the count of source indices that fall below `toOffset`. All three non-trivial test cases I traced manually produce the expected output.
- `normalized` is a clean, stable, two-filter partition. Swift's `filter` is order-preserving, so pinned relative order and unpinned relative order are both maintained.
- `move` correctly handles the pinned/unpinned base offset, and the documented precondition ("Assumes `tabs` already satisfies the pinned-first invariant") is appropriate — enforcing it inside the function would be overengineering.
- Strict discipline: `Foundation`-only (`import Foundation` only), zero SwiftUI, no stray files, exactly two new files, namespace `enum` idiom is idiomatic Swift, doc comments are accurate.
- The `@main` test executable pattern matches the project's existing test convention (confirmed by the verification step).

**Issues:**

- **Minor — `Tests/TabOrderingTests.swift:43`:** The multi-index `fromOffsets` code path in `moving` is not exercised by any test. `IndexSet(integer:)` gives single-element sets in every case. The logic that handles multiple indices (ascending collection + descending removal + `insertionIndex` counting) is correct by inspection, but a multi-element `IndexSet` test would close the only meaningful untested branch. This is a gap worth noting but not a showstopper given YAGNI.
- **Minor — `Tungsten/Sources/Tungsten/Browser/Tabs/TabOrdering.swift:11`:** `tabs.filter { $0.isPinned == false }` mixes styles with `tabs.filter(\.isPinned)` on the line above. Should be `tabs.filter { !$0.isPinned }` or `tabs.filter { $0.isPinned == false }` consistently; the existing codebase uses `== false` elsewhere so this is tolerable but worth standardizing to the `!` prefix or the keypath form (`\.isPinned == false` is not valid keypath syntax in Swift, so `{ !$0.isPinned }` is the natural pair). Not a correctness issue.

**Assessment: APPROVED**

The logic is correct, the discipline is tight, and the tests cover the meaningful behavioral cases. The two minor items (no multi-index test, minor style inconsistency) do not warrant blocking. No must-fix items.

**Strengths:**

- The `moving` helper faithfully re-implements SwiftUI's `RangeReplaceableCollection.move(fromOffsets:toOffset:)` semantics: items are collected before removal, removed in descending-index order (preventing index shift errors), and `insertionIndex` is correctly adjusted by subtracting the count of source indices that fall below `toOffset`. - `normalized` is a clean, stable, two-filter partition. Swift's `filter` is order-preserving, so pinned relative order and unpinned relative order are both maintained.
- `move` correctly handles the pinned/unpinned base offset, and the documented precondition ("Assumes `tabs` already satisfies the pinned-first invariant") is appropriate — enforcing it inside the function would be overengineering.

- **Minor — `Tests/TabOrderingTests.swift:43`:** The multi-index `fromOffsets` code path in `moving` is not exercised by any test. `IndexSet(integer:)` gives single-element sets in every case. The logic that handles multiple indices (ascending collection + descending removal + `insertionIndex` counting) is correct by inspection, but a multi-element `IndexSet` test would close the only meaningful untested branch. This is a gap worth noting but not a showstopper given YAGNI.

Not a correctness issue.

The logic is correct, the discipline is tight, and the tests cover the meaningful behavioral cases. The two minor items (no multi-index test, minor style inconsistency) do not warrant blocking. No must-fix items.

# Final Code Review: Sidebar → NavigationSplitView (`4813313..d2e6b7e`)

## Summary
This is a clean, well-scoped, spec-faithful implementation. The pinned-first invariant and section-relative reorder math are provably correct (I validated `TabOrdering.move` against reference `move(fromOffsets:toOffset:)` semantics across 15 single/multi/non-contiguous cases — all match), the compact/separate layouts are untouched except the one documented pinned-leading side-effect, and the guard reconciliation is exactly the minimal single-line edit the spec promised. No critical or important issues. A few minor polish items and a focused manual-QA list around the native-toolbar/`hiddenTitleBar` interplay, which is the only genuine runtime risk.

## Strengths
- **Correct index mapping.** `TabOrdering.move` computes `pinnedCount = prefix(while: \.isPinned)` and offsets by `base`, which exactly aligns with the two `ForEach`s: `pinnedTabs`/`unpinnedTabs` are `filter`-derived from the same pinned-first array, so section row *i* maps to absolute index `i` (pinned) or `pinnedCount + i` (unpinned). The `ForEach` data and the move math cannot desync because both derive from the single invariant. The hand-rolled `moving` helper matches stdlib semantics.
- **Invariant is closed under all mutations.** `normalizeTabOrder()` is a stable partition and is called at exactly the three sites that can violate it (load, `toggleTabPin`, `reopenLastClosedTab`). `createTab` only appends unpinned (preserves invariant), `closeOtherTabs`/`clearUnpinnedTabs` produce already-ordered results, and `moveTabs` preserves it by construction. `prefix(while:)` in `TabOrdering.move` is therefore always equal to `pinnedTabs.count`.
- **Selection integrity is sound.** The nil-dropping `selectionBinding` prevents empty-area deselection from tearing down the live page via `selectedTabID.didSet`. Reorder mutates only `tabs` order (selection is by id, untouched). Closing the selected row routes through the unchanged `close(_:)`, whose `didSet`-driven next-selection logic is preserved.
- **DRY done right.** `BrowserContentView` cleanly extracts the shared session/start-page switch; the toolbar reuses the in-place-promoted controls verbatim with no behavior change.
- **A2 deviation correctly confined.** `NavigationSplitView`, `ToolbarItem`, and `ToolbarItemGroup` appear *only* in `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift`. I ran `ThreadBrowserLifecycleTests.sh` — it passes, and the only guard edit is the removed `SidebarBrowserChrome` line. No stale references to `SidebarBrowserChrome`/`sidebarWidth` remain anywhere.

## Issues

### Minor
1. **`AddressField`'s `.frame(maxHeight: .infinity)` reused inside a fixed-height toolbar item** — `BrowserChrome.swift:305`, consumed at `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift:27-28`. The shared field ends in `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity, alignment: .top)`, designed for the floating chrome where an outer fixed `.frame(height:)` bounds it. In the toolbar principal item only width is constrained; the `maxHeight: .infinity` relies on the toolbar's intrinsic row height to bound it. This will almost certainly look fine (toolbars impose their own height), but it's the single reused-control seam most likely to render oddly (e.g., the field's rounded background stretching). Fix if QA shows it: add `.frame(height: ChromeMetrics.controlHeight)` to the `AddressField` in `SidebarBrowserLayout` (spec §Decision 6 already calls for fixed-height here).

2. **Redundant `.toolbar(removing: .title)`** — applied both on the `ZStack` in `BrowserSplitView.swift:57` (all layouts) and again on the `NavigationSplitView` in `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift:21`. Harmless (idempotent), but the inner one is technically redundant. Leave as-is — it documents intent locally and removing it would couple the two files. Not worth a change.

3. **`columnVisibility` is `@State`, so collapse/width state is per-window-instance, not persisted across launches.** Spec acceptance criteria say "drag-to-resize (persisted)". Column *width* with `.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth` is persisted by the system via the window frame autosave; the `.all` initial `columnVisibility` just sets the default-open state, which is the conventional choice. This is fine and matches normal `NavigationSplitView` usage — flagging only so the QA driver explicitly confirms width survives relaunch (criterion calls it out).

### Non-issues I checked and cleared
- **No dead code from the removed rail.** `ChromeMetrics.sidebarWidth` deleted; `totalHeight(for: .sidebar)` correctly retained returning `0` (still called unconditionally at `BrowserSplitView.swift:18` and used for the find-bar offset, which is correct — sidebar mode's find bar sits at `chromeHeight + 8 = 8`).
- **`>60` tabs `suffix`-capping drops leading (pinned) tabs on persist.** I verified this logic is **identical at base commit 4813313** — pre-existing, not a regression. Pinned-first ordering makes it marginally more visible, but it's out of scope and the invariant still holds on reload via `normalizeTabOrder()`.
- **The working-tree `M` files in `git status`** (ThreadModelTests, AppPreferences, BrowserChrome, ChromeMetrics, BrowserSplitView, GeneralSettingsView, ThreadBrowserLifecycleTests.sh) are uncommitted changes *not part of this range* — `git diff 4813313..d2e6b7e` for ThreadModelTests is empty and the branch tip is clean. They belong to a separate/parallel effort; the reviewed commits do not include them.

## Manual-QA watch list (cannot be unit-tested)
1. **`hiddenTitleBar` ↔ native toolbar (primary risk).** Confirm the toolbar actually renders, traffic lights are correctly positioned, and the address/nav/action items are visible and not clipped — in **both light and dark**, and with Reduce Transparency on. `SafariWindowChromeConfigurator` sets `titleVisibility=.hidden` + `fullSizeContentView` for all layouts; verify it doesn't suppress the sidebar toolbar.
2. **CEF detail occlusion with `topInset: 0`.** The detail pane passes `topInset: 0` (toolbar reserves its own height). Confirm the top of the web page is not hidden under the toolbar.
3. **AddressField height in the toolbar** (see Minor #1) — check the field isn't vertically stretched/misshapen.
4. **No selection-reactivation loop.** Select tabs rapidly and reorder the *selected* row; confirm the page doesn't reactivate/flicker (the binding reflecting programmatic `selectedTabID` back into the `List` should be inert since the getter just reads the model).
5. **Drag-reorder persistence round-trip.** Reorder within Pinned and within Tabs, quit, relaunch — order should survive (`moveTabs` → `persistTabs` → `BrowserTabSnapshot`, which stores tabs in array order).
6. **Pinned section show/hide.** Unpin the last pinned tab → "Pinned" section header disappears; pin one → it reappears and the tab jumps to the top.
7. **Close-from-row + last-tab.** Close the selected unpinned row via its hover `xmark`; closing the final tab should auto-create a new one (unchanged `close(_:)`).
8. **Compact/Separate regression check.** Switch back; confirm strips look unchanged aside from pinned tabs now sorting leading (`TabStrip`/`InlineTabStrip` iterate `browserModel.tabs`, now pinned-first).

# Final Code Review: Sidebar → NavigationSplitView (`4813313..d2e6b7e`)

## Summary
This is a clean, well-scoped, spec-faithful implementation. The pinned-first invariant and section-relative reorder math are provably correct (I validated `TabOrdering.move` against reference `move(fromOffsets:toOffset:)` semantics across 15 single/multi/non-contiguous cases — all match), the compact/separate layouts are untouched except the one documented pinned-leading side-effect, and the guard reconciliation is exactly the minimal single-line edit the spec promised. No critical or important issues. A few minor polish items and a focused manual-QA list around the native-toolbar/`hiddenTitleBar` interplay, which is the only genuine runtime risk.

## Strengths
- **Correct index mapping.** `TabOrdering.move` computes `pinnedCount = prefix(while: \.isPinned)` and offsets by `base`, which exactly aligns with the two `ForEach`s: `pinnedTabs`/`unpinnedTabs` are `filter`-derived from the same pinned-first array, so section row *i* maps to absolute index `i` (pinned) or `pinnedCount + i` (unpinned). The `ForEach` data and the move math cannot desync because both derive from the single invariant. The hand-rolled `moving` helper matches stdlib semantics.
- **Invariant is closed under all mutations.** `normalizeTabOrder()` is a stable partition and is called at exactly the three sites that can violate it (load, `toggleTabPin`, `reopenLastClosedTab`). `createTab` only appends unpinned (preserves invariant), `closeOtherTabs`/`clearUnpinnedTabs` produce already-ordered results, and `moveTabs` preserves it by construction. `prefix(while:)` in `TabOrdering.move` is therefore always equal to `pinnedTabs.count`.
- **Selection integrity is sound.** The nil-dropping `selectionBinding` prevents empty-area deselection from tearing down the live page via `selectedTabID.didSet`. Reorder mutates only `tabs` order (selection is by id, untouched). Closing the selected row routes through the unchanged `close(_:)`, whose `didSet`-driven next-selection logic is preserved.
- **DRY done right.** `BrowserContentView` cleanly extracts the shared session/start-page switch; the toolbar reuses the in-place-promoted controls verbatim with no behavior change.
- **A2 deviation correctly confined.** `NavigationSplitView`, `ToolbarItem`, and `ToolbarItemGroup` appear *only* in `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift`. I ran `ThreadBrowserLifecycleTests.sh` — it passes, and the only guard edit is the removed `SidebarBrowserChrome` line. No stale references to `SidebarBrowserChrome`/`sidebarWidth` remain anywhere.

## Issues

### Minor
1. **`AddressField`'s `.frame(maxHeight: .infinity)` reused inside a fixed-height toolbar item** — `BrowserChrome.swift:305`, consumed at `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift:27-28`. The shared field ends in `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity, alignment: .top)`, designed for the floating chrome where an outer fixed `.frame(height:)` bounds it. In the toolbar principal item only width is constrained; the `maxHeight: .infinity` relies on the toolbar's intrinsic row height to bound it. This will almost certainly look fine (toolbars impose their own height), but it's the single reused-control seam most likely to render oddly (e.g., the field's rounded background stretching). Fix if QA shows it: add `.frame(height: ChromeMetrics.controlHeight)` to the `AddressField` in `SidebarBrowserLayout` (spec §Decision 6 already calls for fixed-height here).

2. **Redundant `.toolbar(removing: .title)`** — applied both on the `ZStack` in `BrowserSplitView.swift:57` (all layouts) and again on the `NavigationSplitView` in `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift:21`. Harmless (idempotent), but the inner one is technically redundant. Leave as-is — it documents intent locally and removing it would couple the two files. Not worth a change.

3. **`columnVisibility` is `@State`, so collapse/width state is per-window-instance, not persisted across launches.** Spec acceptance criteria say "drag-to-resize (persisted)". Column *width* with `.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth` is persisted by the system via the window frame autosave; the `.all` initial `columnVisibility` just sets the default-open state, which is the conventional choice. This is fine and matches normal `NavigationSplitView` usage — flagging only so the QA driver explicitly confirms width survives relaunch (criterion calls it out).

### Non-issues I checked and cleared
- **No dead code from the removed rail.** `ChromeMetrics.sidebarWidth` deleted; `totalHeight(for: .sidebar)` correctly retained returning `0` (still called unconditionally at `BrowserSplitView.swift:18` and used for the find-bar offset, which is correct — sidebar mode's find bar sits at `chromeHeight + 8 = 8`).
- **`>60` tabs `suffix`-capping drops leading (pinned) tabs on persist.** I verified this logic is **identical at base commit 4813313** — pre-existing, not a regression. Pinned-first ordering makes it marginally more visible, but it's out of scope and the invariant still holds on reload via `normalizeTabOrder()`.
- **The working-tree `M` files in `git status`** (ThreadModelTests, AppPreferences, BrowserChrome, ChromeMetrics, BrowserSplitView, GeneralSettingsView, ThreadBrowserLifecycleTests.sh) are uncommitted changes *not part of this range* — `git diff 4813313..d2e6b7e` for ThreadModelTests is empty and the branch tip is clean. They belong to a separate/parallel effort; the reviewed commits do not include them.

## Manual-QA watch list (cannot be unit-tested)
1. **`hiddenTitleBar` ↔ native toolbar (primary risk).** Confirm the toolbar actually renders, traffic lights are correctly positioned, and the address/nav/action items are visible and not clipped — in **both light and dark**, and with Reduce Transparency on. `SafariWindowChromeConfigurator` sets `titleVisibility=.hidden` + `fullSizeContentView` for all layouts; verify it doesn't suppress the sidebar toolbar.
2. **CEF detail occlusion with `topInset: 0`.** The detail pane passes `topInset: 0` (toolbar reserves its own height). Confirm the top of the web page is not hidden under the toolbar.
3. **AddressField height in the toolbar** (see Minor #1) — check the field isn't vertically stretched/misshapen.
4. **No selection-reactivation loop.** Select tabs rapidly and reorder the *selected* row; confirm the page doesn't reactivate/flicker (the binding reflecting programmatic `selectedTabID` back into the `List` should be inert since the getter just reads the model).
5. **Drag-reorder persistence round-trip.** Reorder within Pinned and within Tabs, quit, relaunch — order should survive (`moveTabs` → `persistTabs` → `BrowserTabSnapshot`, which stores tabs in array order).
6. **Pinned section show/hide.** Unpin the last pinned tab → "Pinned" section header disappears; pin one → it reappears and the tab jumps to the top.
7. **Close-from-row + last-tab.** Close the selected unpinned row via its hover `xmark`; closing the final tab should auto-create a new one (unchanged `close(_:)`).
8. **Compact/Separate regression check.** Switch back; confirm strips look unchanged aside from pinned tabs now sorting leading (`TabStrip`/`InlineTabStrip` iterate `browserModel.tabs`, now pinned-first).

## Verdict
**READY TO MERGE.** No critical or important issues; the invariant and reorder logic are correct and the deviation is properly confined and documented. The Minor items are optional polish, with Minor #1 (AddressField fixed height) the only one likely to need a one-line follow-up *if* manual QA shows the field rendering oddly in the toolbar — which is exactly what the QA watch list exists to catch.

**Final review: READY TO MERGE.** The opus reviewer validated the reorder math against 15 cases, confirmed the pinned-first invariant is closed under every mutation, selection integrity holds, the A2 deviation is properly confined to `SidebarBrowserLayout.swift`, and no dead code remains. No critical/important issues — three optional minors, the only notable one being that the toolbar address field relies on intrinsic toolbar height (spec's "fixed height"), which is a *visual* thing best confirmed by eye.

content.text:
Confirmed — and the key enabler is real: the CEF web view already supports corner rounding. In [TungstenCEFBridge.mm:1451](Tungsten/Sources/Tungsten/CEF/TungstenCEFBridge.mm#L1451), `setCornerRadius` sets `view.layer.cornerRadius` + `masksToBounds`, and `BrowserDetailView` currently just pins it to `0`. So **yes, this is fully doable with native elements** — no hacks:

- **Rounded content card** → set `controller.cornerRadius` (~10–12) and inset `BrowserDetailView` with padding. The window is already transparent glass (`isOpaque = false`), so the margins/gap reveal the backing.
- **Detached controls** → the chrome is already a `.glassEffect` bar; it just needs to float above the card instead of sitting flush.
- **Animated gap** → there's already an `isExpanded` state driving the expand-on-type; the gap is just another value animated off it.

On the inverse gap: the elegant version is to keep the **content card's top edge from jumping** — as the bar grows on focus it "breathes" *down into* the gap (expanded = tall bar, tight gap), and on collapse the bar shrinks and the gap opens back up. Same content position, just the bar and gap trading space. (Say if you'd rather the page itself shift up/down instead.)

Two things I'll need your eyes on once it's running (I can't see it): whether CEF **clips cleanly** at the rounded corners (the property's wired, but GPU-composited web content can occasionally overshoot a rounded mask — if so there's a fallback), and **traffic-light placement** once the bar detaches.

One fork decides how much I touch, so:

options.description: Round + inset the web content into a floating card; keep the glass control bar full-width across the very top (traffic lights stay on it as today) with the animated gap between the bar and the card. Delivers the rounded-window + gap + controls-on-top look with the least risk — no macOS traffic-light surgery. Good first iteration we can push further.

options.label: Fully floating pill bar
options.description: The control bar also detaches into a pill with margins on all sides (Arc-style), and the macOS traffic lights relocate into the top-left gap above the card. Closest to a fully 'detached' look, but the traffic-light positioning under hiddenTitleBar needs careful handling and more visual back-and-forth.

7	/// `NSColor.separatorColor`, system fills, …) so it adapts to light/dark, the
8	/// user's accent color, and accessibility settings automatically.
9	enum ChromeMetrics {
10	    /// Main toolbar row height. Compact single row with the traffic lights
11	    /// inline (Safari-style); the glass spans the full top.
12	    static let barHeight: CGFloat = 50
13	    /// Dedicated tab-strip height in the `.separate` layout.
14	    static let tabBarHeight: CGFloat = 38
15	
16	    /// Interactive control height inside the bar (buttons, address field).
17	    static let controlHeight: CGFloat = 28
18	    /// Tab height.
19	    static let tabHeight: CGFloat = 28
20	
21	    /// Address-field height when focused — it grows from `controlHeight` in
22	    /// place (same position, same corner radius), nothing else moves.
23	    static let expandedFieldHeight: CGFloat = 56
24	    /// Tab height when minimized to a thin bar (focused state) — the tab
25	    /// shrinks vertically, keeping its width.
26	    static let minimizedTabHeight: CGFloat = 12
27	
28	    /// Leading inset that keeps chrome clear of the window traffic lights.
29	    static let trafficLightGutter: CGFloat = 78
30	
31	    /// SF Symbol point size for bar controls.
32	    static let iconSize: CGFloat = 14
33	    static let smallIconSize: CGFloat = 11
34	
35	    /// macOS body / compact text sizes.
36	    static let bodyFontSize: CGFloat = 13
37	    static let compactFontSize: CGFloat = 12
38	
39	    /// Corner radius for control hover / selection fills.
40	    static let controlCornerRadius: CGFloat = 7
41	
42	    /// Total chrome height for a given tab layout.
43	    static func totalHeight(for layout: BrowserTabLayout) -> CGFloat {
44	        layout == .separate ? barHeight + tabBarHeight : barHeight
45	    }
46	}

Relaunched (older instance quit first). Here's what you should be seeing — and again, I can't see it, so I need your read:

**The layout now**
- The web page is a **rounded card** (≈12pt corners), inset ~10pt from the window's sides and bottom; the window backing shows around it.
- The glass control bar floats full-width across the top, **bottom corners rounded**, hairline separator gone — it reads as a detached slab above the card.
- A **gap** sits between the bar and the card, and it **breathes**: focus the address bar / type → the bar grows down and the gap tightens (~8pt); click away or let it idle-collapse → the bar shrinks and the gap opens back up (~36pt). The card holds its position — no jump.
- The new-tab **start page** is the same rounded card.

**What I most need you to check**
1. **CEF corner clipping** (the risk I flagged): do the *web page's* corners actually clip cleanly to the rounded card, or does content overshoot the rounded mask at the corners? If it overshoots, that's the GPU-compositing case and I'll switch to a masking fallback.
2. **What shows in the gap/margins** — with translucency **off** it's the adaptive solid window color; **on**, it may be the raw desktop. Say if you'd rather a defined surface there.
3. **Numbers to nudge** — gap (36→8), margins (10), card radius (12), bar bottom radius (12). Too much / too little?

Nothing's committed (uncommitted on `main`). How does it look — especially #1 — and what should I tune?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

CEF_CURRENT="${SRCROOT}/../Vendor/CEF/current"
ARTI_VENDOR_BIN="${SRCROOT}/../Vendor/Arti/bin/arti"
FRAMEWORKS_DIR="${TARGET_BUILD_DIR}/${FRAMEWORKS_FOLDER_PATH}"
RESOURCES_DIR="${TARGET_BUILD_DIR}/${UNLOCALIZED_RESOURCES_FOLDER_PATH}"
ARTI_RESOURCE_BIN="${RESOURCES_DIR}/Arti/arti"
APP_INFO_PLIST="${TARGET_BUILD_DIR}/${INFOPLIST_PATH:-${WRAPPER_NAME}/Contents/Info.plist}"

if [[ ! -d "${CEF_CURRENT}" ]]; then
  echo "Missing CEF runtime at ${CEF_CURRENT}." >&2
  echo "Run ./scripts/setup-cef.sh --arch arm64 from the repository root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

CEF_RUNTIME_CONFIGURATION="${CEF_RUNTIME_CONFIGURATION:-Release}"
FRAMEWORK_SRC="${CEF_CURRENT}/${CEF_RUNTIME_CONFIGURATION}/Chromium Embedded Framework.framework"

HELPER_NAMES=(
  "Tungsten Helper"
  "Tungsten Helper (Alerts)"
  "Tungsten Helper (GPU)"
  "Tungsten Helper (Plugin)"
  "Tungsten Helper (Renderer)"
)

if [[ ! -d "${FRAMEWORK_SRC}" ]]; then
  echo "Missing ${CEF_RUNTIME_CONFIGURATION} Chromium Embedded Framework.framework in ${CEF_CURRENT}." >&2
  exit 1
fi

for helper_name in "${HELPER_NAMES[@]}"; do
  if [[ ! -d "${CEF_CURRENT}/build/${helper_name}.app" ]]; then
    echo "Missing ${helper_name}.app. Run ./scripts/setup-cef.sh --arch arm64 again." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done

mkdir -p "${FRAMEWORKS_DIR}"

rm -rf "${FRAMEWORKS_DIR}/Chromium Embedded Framework.framework"
rm -rf "${FRAMEWORKS_DIR}"/Tungsten\ Helper*.app

CEF_FRAMEWORK_DST="${FRAMEWORKS_DIR}/Chromium Embedded Framework.framework"
CEF_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_DST="${CEF_FRAMEWORK_DST}/Versions/A"

mkdir -p "${CEF_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_DST}"
ditto "${FRAMEWORK_SRC}/Chromium Embedded Framework" "${CEF_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_DST}/Chromium Embedded Framework"
ditto "${FRAMEWORK_SRC}/Resources" "${CEF_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_DST}/Resources"
ditto "${FRAMEWORK_SRC}/Libraries" "${CEF_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_DST}/Libraries"

ln -sfn A "${CEF_FRAMEWORK_DST}/Versions/Current"

file.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ROOT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
DERIVED_DATA="${TUNGSTEN_DERIVED_DATA:-/tmp/TungstenDerivedData}"
APP_VERSION="${TUNGSTEN_VERSION:-0.12}"
BUILD_NUMBER="${TUNGSTEN_BUILD_NUMBER:-$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)}"
ARTI_VENDOR_BIN="${ROOT_DIR}/Vendor/Arti/bin/arti"
APP_PATH="${DERIVED_DATA}/Build/Products/Release/Tungsten.app"
APP_ARTI_BIN="${APP_PATH}/Contents/Resources/Arti/arti"

cd "$ROOT_DIR"

if [[ ! -x "$ARTI_VENDOR_BIN" ]]; then
  echo "Arti not found at $ARTI_VENDOR_BIN; running setup-arti.sh..."
  "${ROOT_DIR}/scripts/setup-arti.sh"
fi

xcodebuild \
  -project Tungsten/Tungsten.xcodeproj \
  -scheme Tungsten \
  -configuration Release \
  -destination 'platform=macOS' \
  -derivedDataPath "$DERIVED_DATA" \
  MARKETING_VERSION="$APP_VERSION" \
  CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION="$BUILD_NUMBER" \
  "$@" \
  build

if [[ ! -x "$APP_ARTI_BIN" ]]; then
  echo "Release build did not embed Arti at $APP_ARTI_BIN." >&2
  echo "Run ./scripts/setup-arti.sh and build again." >&2
  exit 1
fi

/System/Library/Frameworks/CoreServices.framework/Frameworks/LaunchServices.framework/Support/lsregister \
  -f -R "$APP_PATH" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

echo
echo "Built: $APP_PATH"
echo "Version: $APP_VERSION ($BUILD_NUMBER)"
echo "Bundled Arti: $APP_ARTI_BIN"

name: tungsten_build_run_verify
description: "How to build, run, and visually verify the Tungsten macOS app"

Tungsten is a native macOS SwiftUI + CEF browser. Build the debug app with `./scripts/build-debug.sh` (CEF binaries live in `Vendor/CEF`; derived data goes to `/tmp/TungstenDerivedData`, app at `/tmp/TungstenDerivedData/Build/Products/Debug/Tungsten.app`).

The Xcode project uses **file-system-synchronized groups**, so new `.swift` files under `Tungsten/Tungsten/` compile automatically — no `.pbxproj` edits needed.
